orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, carrying straight on from Isabella's letter in Chapter XIII, in the early spring of 1784. At the very end, after the row of asterisks, Lockwood takes over again with a few lines of his own as Nelly goes down to meet the doctor.

notes.m: 'Peruse' means to read thoroughly, not to skim. An 'epistle' is a letter.

notes.g: A sign of forgiveness, sent through me: a note or keepsake.

notes.t: It is out of the question
should she really wish to oblige me
notes.g: If she really wants to do me a favour.

notes.m: 'Country' here means the district or neighbourhood, not the nation.

notes.t: Mr. Edgar’s coldness depressed me exceedingly
notes.g: Edgar's coldness made me very sad.
The window, made of small panes held in a criss-cross frame.
The paved path up through the garden.
Wuthering Heights, which was a happier place when Nelly lived there.

notes.t: partook of the pervading spirit of neglect which encompassed her
notes.g: Had caught the general air of neglect around her.
Hindley Earnshaw, Catherine's brother and master of Wuthering Heights.
A small leather wallet or folder for papers and notes.
notes.m: Not a pocket-sized book to read, and not a woman's purse.
About appearance here, not moral goodness.

notes.g: A gentleman from birth and by upbringing.
notes.n: Strong praise: Heathcliff was a foundling with no family name (Chapter IV).

notes.g: A real little slob; a messy, untidy woman.
A long low cabinet for dishes, against a dining-room wall.
A woman's hat tied under the chin.

notes.m: A time word, not 'in a straight line'.

notes.n: Heathcliff uses her familiar name; Isabella calls her Ellen.
Careful: in Chapters I to IV, 'Mrs. Heathcliff' was the young woman Lockwood met at the Heights in 1801. Here, in 1784, it means Isabella.

notes.g: The flat stone floor in front of a fireplace.
Sharp questioning, like a lawyer questioning a witness in court.

notes.n: Catherine's illness began after the quarrel between Heathcliff and Edgar in Chapter XI.

notes.t: if you really have a regard for her
notes.g: If you really care for her.
notes.m: 'Regard' here means affection, not just respect or attention.

notes.g: Keep up his love from now on.
Force a promise out of you.

notes.m: Not a formal question session: any face-to-face meeting.

notes.n: 'Gall' is bile, a byword for bitterness. In the Bible, Jesus is offered vinegar mixed with gall on the cross.

notes.g: The moment she stopped caring for him.
Moral doubts that stop you doing something.

notes.t: At a most miserable period of my life
notes.g: During the worst time of my life.
notes.n: Probably the three years he was away, after overhearing Catherine say it would degrade her to marry him (Chapter IX).

notes.g: When Heathcliff came back, in Chapter X.

notes.t: Two words would comprehend my future
notes.g: Two words would sum up my future.

notes.n: 'Death and hell' are paired several times in the Bible's Book of Revelation. Heathcliff means life without Catherine would be hell.
'Puny' means weak and small.

notes.g: A long open box of water for horses to drink from.

notes.t: turns you adrift on the world
notes.g: Casts you out on your own.
Isabella, whom Nelly served at the Grange.

notes.n: 'Condition' meant your position in life, such as single or married.

notes.g: A complete slob; a dirty, untidy woman.
notes.m: No sexual meaning here: a 'slut' was a woman careless about cleanliness. Still harsh and insulting.

notes.t: the very morrow of our wedding
notes.g: The very day after our wedding.

notes.m: 'Nice' meant particular, dainty, fastidious, not pleasant.
'Abroad' meant out of the house, not in a foreign country.

notes.g: The only girl in the family.
A hero from a romantic novel.
notes.n: 'Romance' meant a story of love and adventure. Heathcliff says Isabella fell for an imaginary dashing hero.

notes.g: A thinking being; someone capable of reason.

notes.t: a fabulous notion of my character
notes.g: An imaginary, fairy-tale idea of what I'm like.

notes.n: In Greek myth, the hero Hercules had to perform twelve near-impossible 'labours'. Heathcliff mocks how hard it was to make her hate him.

notes.g: If it really has been done.

notes.t: to hang up her little dog
notes.g: Heathcliff hanged Isabella's dog as they left the Grange.
notes.n: In Chapter XII Nelly found Isabella's springer spaniel, Fanny, hanging by a handkerchief and nearly dead.
He means Catherine, though Isabella may have thought he meant her.
An old word, used here as a savage insult.

notes.g: Just because I ran out of ideas.
Edgar's brotherly heart, and his heart as a magistrate.
notes.n: Edgar is a local magistrate, or justice of the peace, as his father was (Chapter VI). Heathcliff sneers that he is staying just inside the law.

notes.t: I keep strictly within the limits of the law
notes.n: A husband then had wide legal power over his wife. Only proven serious cruelty or adultery could get a wife a legal separation.

notes.g: Apply for a legal separation from her husband.
notes.n: Divorce was almost impossible, and very costly. A church court could grant a separation, but the couple stayed married and neither could remarry.

notes.t: the gratification to be derived from tormenting her
notes.g: The pleasure I get from tormenting her.
Take advantage of being allowed to go.

notes.n: 'Ire' means anger.
Through Isabella, Heathcliff may have a claim on the Linton property (see Chapters X and XIII).

notes.t: If you are called upon in a court of law
notes.g: If you're ever made a witness in court.
notes.n: Heathcliff hints that Isabella's wild words could be used to show she is unstable, and so needs her husband's control.

notes.t: she’s near the point which would suit me
notes.g: She's close to the state I want.
notes.n: He may mean close to madness, which would let him treat her as unfit to manage herself.

notes.t: not fit to be your own guardian
notes.g: Not able to look after yourself.
Your husband, who has legal control of you.
notes.n: Under English law ('coverture') a wife had no separate legal identity: her husband was responsible for her and controlled her property and person.

notes.t: I have something to say to Ellen Dean in private
notes.g: Ellen Dean is Nelly's full name.

notes.t: Why, this is the road upstairs, child!
notes.n: Heathcliff mocks her as he shoves her out.

notes.g: It is like a baby teething, but in the mind.
notes.n: A teething baby bites harder as the pain grows. Heathcliff says the more others suffer, the harder he wants to grind.

notes.g: Quickly putting my hat back on.
notes.m: 'Resume' means take up again, here pick up and wear the hat she took off.

notes.g: Keep coming back to the place.

notes.n: 'Insure' was an old spelling of 'ensure'.

notes.g: The house of the man I work for (Edgar).
I argued; I pressed the point.

notes.m: 'Inmates' meant residents of any house, not prisoners.

notes.g: People watching her on Edgar's behalf.

notes.t: plant an oak in a flower-pot
notes.g: Try to grow a huge tree in a tiny pot.
notes.n: Heathcliff's image: Catherine's nature is too big for Edgar's 'shallow' care to nourish.
A footman waited at table, opened doors and attended the family. Keeping one was a sign of a well-off household.

notes.t: I engaged to carry a letter
notes.g: I promised to deliver a letter.
Word of the next time Edgar would be away.
Useful or convenient, though not strictly right.
A turning point for the better.
notes.n: Doctors then spoke of an illness reaching a 'crisis', after which the patient either recovered or got worse.

notes.g: Telling tales; reporting what other people say and do.
By repeating it to myself again and again.

notes.t: ere I could prevail on myself

notes.g: Mr. Kenneth, the local doctor, who is treating Lockwood.

notes.t: My history is dree, as we say
notes.g: My story is long and gloomy, as we say around here.
notes.n: 'Dree' is a northern dialect word meaning tedious, dreary. Nelly marks it as a local word for Lockwood.

notes.g: Pass the time on another morning.
Lockwood picks up Nelly's dialect word 'dree' and adds the standard 'dreary'.

notes.t: extract wholesome medicines from Mrs. Dean’s bitter herbs
notes.g: Get a healthy lesson out of Nelly's grim story.
notes.n: Lockwood, a patient full of medicines, treats her tale like a bitter herbal remedy that does you good.

notes.m: Stronger than mere interest: to 'fascinate' once meant to bewitch, as a snake was said to freeze its prey.

notes.g: The eyes of young Mrs. Heathcliff, whom Lockwood met at the Heights.
notes.n: This is the younger Catherine of 1801, the daughter Nelly mentioned in Chapter IV. Lockwood finds her very attractive.

notes.g: In a strange fix; in a fine state.
notes.n: 'A taking' meant a state of agitation.

notes.t: a second edition of the mother
notes.g: A copy of her mother, the first Catherine.
notes.n: Lockwood worries the daughter might be as wild as the mother in Nelly's story.
